source: Ward, Patterson, Sifonis, Dodds, Saunders (2002) The role of graded category structure in imaginative thought, Memory & Cognition 30(2)
finding: People who imagine alien animals start from an Earth animal that comes to mind easily. The more often an animal is listed first by others, the more often it is used as a base for an imaginary creature.
numbers: Exp 1A: 30 people listed animals, 147 distinct animals. Exp 1B: 71 people drew alien creatures; 45 (63%) named a specific Earth animal, about two thirds counting vague ones; 32 distinct animals named. Correlation of imagination frequency with output dominance r about .49 (full set), .68 (items listed by 5 or more). Creatures: 99% had a sensory organ, 97% an appendage, 91% bilateral symmetry. Originality (7-point): those who named an Earth animal 3.18 vs 4.34 who did not, t(69)=2.81, p<.01.
quote: those items that come to mind most readily are the ones most likely to serve as starting points for the development of novel ideas
limits: One lab, undergraduates, retrospective self-report of sources (coded from text). Human is the exception (used by 12 of 71, listed by 1 of 30). Originality rated by coders.
agent_relevance: Closes the Ward gap in part: the effect is large and retrievability-driven. For an LLM the analogue is the highest-probability prototype; sampling an alien category will mostly return Earth parts. Test by counting default features in model output.

source: Ward et al. (2002) Experiment 2, imaginary tools for a creature with no appendages
finding: A hard task constraint did not stop people using Earth tools as the base. They kept the Earth tool and patched it.
numbers: 135 people (control vs no-appendages). 68% named a specific Earth tool (64% control, 72% constrained). Constrained group: handles on 23% vs 73% of tools (chi2(1,135)=33.20), mouth pieces 39% vs 1%, harnesses 20% vs 3%. Those who named an Earth tool: originality 3.03 vs 4.18, t(133)=4.25, p<.001.
limits: Constraint forced adaptation, not abandonment; originality of the patched tool still lower. Single lab.
agent_relevance: A constraint changes surface features but not the starting prototype. For O4 (drop or add a constraint), expect patched copies of the default approach unless the default approach itself is banned or removed from context.

source: Ward et al. (2002) Experiment 4, imaginary fruit with creativity instructions
finding: Telling people to be creative did not reduce reliance on Earth exemplars. Telling them they need not be bound by Earth fruit reduced it, but not to zero.
numbers: 203 people across control, creative, not-bound. Reliance on Earth fruit: 66% control, 62% creative (ns), 48% not-bound (chi2(1,N=153)=4.56, p<.05 vs control). Originality: reliance 2.50 vs no reliance 3.40, F(1,197)=34.51, p<.001; condition F(2,197)=5.78 (control 2.57, creative 3.12, not-bound 3.16).
limits: Instruction effect is modest; originality gain from instruction is about half a scale point.
agent_relevance: 'Be creative' prompts barely work; a targeted release from the default category worked more than a generic one. Supports using a specific permission or ban over a generic novelty request (K16, K19).

source: Ward (1994) Structured imagination: the role of category structure in exemplar generation, Cognitive Psychology 27, as reported in Ward et al. (2002)
finding: The 1994 paper itself was not found open. What Ward 2002 reports: students inventing alien animals still gave them eyes, legs and bilateral symmetry even when told to use their wildest imagination; science fiction authors showed the same pattern; Ward and Sifonis 1997 found it again when told to make creatures wildly different; 19% of source statements named films or books.
numbers: Only the 2002 text was read. Percentages 99/97/91 are from the 2002 replication, which says they are comparable to 1994 and Ward and Sifonis 1997.
limits: Second-hand for the 1994 numbers. Original N and exact percentages not verified.
agent_relevance: Treat the structured imagination claim as replicated by the same lab, not as independent. Gap 7 is closed for the human numbers (d01 to d03) but not for the 1994 paper, and no LLM study was found.

source: George and Wiley (2020) Need something different? Here's what's been done: effects of examples and task instructions on creative idea generation, Memory & Cognition 48
finding: Alternate uses task. Verbal common examples plus an avoid-these instruction raised original ideas. Examples alone did not help. Visual examples reduced originality (fixation) and the avoid instruction only brought it back to the no-example level.
numbers: Exp 1: N about 144 (df 140), 2x2 examples x avoid. Original ideas: avoid 2.68 vs no avoid 1.88; examples 2.65 vs no examples (lower); Examples+Avoid greatest vs all others, t(142)=3.51, p=.001, d=0.58. Examples without avoid: no gain (planned t(142)=0.97, ns). Participants without examples spontaneously gave 1.77 of the example ideas; with avoid the share of example ideas fell (M .17 vs .27).
limits: Alternate uses task, not parts-to-object; verbal vs visual modality matters; Exp 2 details not extracted.
agent_relevance: A prior-attempt list works only when paired with an explicit avoid instruction and given as text. This matches NoveltyBench's finding and helps reconcile it with Smith and Marsh (those showed pictures without avoid; see K03).

source: Grammenos and Lubart (2026) Are Eight Chatbots Better Than One? Boosting chatbot creative outcomes via exposure to self- and peer-generated examples (preprint)
finding: Eight chatbots saw their own and peers' earlier outputs. Pick and Mix (combine parts of examples) raised scores on the Divergent Association Task and Alternative Uses Test. Try to Beat mostly failed. The authors say chatbots pick the best candidate well but struggle to reuse its features to make better new ones.
numbers: 8 chatbots, two rounds, five iterations each, two tasks; Friedman tests across the seven steps significant in both rounds (chi2(6,N=8)=33.38 and 31.34, p<.001); the same two steps (4.1, 3.1) ranked best in both rounds.
limits: Preprint, consumer chatbots with unknown settings, scores are fluency-type creativity tests, not checkable outcomes. Not a direct feature-copy measure.
agent_relevance: Showing earlier output can help if the instruction is to recombine, and not help if it is to beat. Instruction wording, not mere exposure, sets the direction. Run both arms in the overlap experiment.

source: Verma (2026) Try Again, Don't Look Back: Blind Resampling Outperforms Self-Repair in Small Code Models (preprint)
finding: Showing a small code model its own failed program makes the next try a near copy. A blind fresh resample beat feedback repair at 1.5B and 3B, and tied at 7B, for fewer tokens. A content-free wrong notice did as well as real execution feedback.
numbers: MBPP+ (378 tasks), Qwen2.5-Coder 1.5B, 3B, 7B plus DeepSeek-Coder 1.3B and 6.7B; k=8 matched budget; pass@1 paired McNemar with Holm. 1.5B: resample .749, feedback penalty -6.1 points (p=0.006). 3B: resample .778, placebo .709, feedback .735, reflect .743. 7B: resample .820, placebo .802, feedback .810, reflect .828 (reflection +0.8, ns, at 2.5x tokens). Near-identical retries (similarity over .95): 33-68% when shown own attempt vs 2-14% blind. Similarity rises .30-.38. Penalty tracks baseline quality (r=.96 over six configs).
quote: Shown its own code, the model edits instead of rethinking
limits: Single author preprint, independent researcher, small open models, one main benchmark (MBPP+), code only. Unreplicated. Own-attempt similarity is a string measure.
agent_relevance: Direct answer to gap 6 and part of gap 4: a model does copy its own earlier attempt in context, and the copy costs accuracy. Default S5 to a fresh resample unless the feedback is specific, and quantify anchoring by similarity between consecutive attempts.

finding: Putting two solved programs for other tasks in the prompt did not change pass@1 within 3.5 points, so the harm in d07 comes from self-conditioning, not longer context.
numbers: Table 2 pass@1 none/random/retrieved: 1.5B .566/.542/.542; 3B .598/.595/.606; 7B .709/.728/.696. All nine paired contrasts ns after Holm.
limits: BM25 retrieval of tasks with little overlap (1.2-1.7% of exemplars over .8 similar to the reference). Does not cover case-based reasoning where the exemplar is close.
agent_relevance: Cross-task memory is safe to add; own-attempt memory needs care. Separates the Smith/Marsh style example effect (close exemplars) from plain context length.

source: Olausson, Inala, Wang, Gao, Solar-Lezama (2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation? ICLR 2024
finding: When repair cost is counted, self-repair gains are modest, vary by problem set, and are sometimes absent. The bottleneck is the quality of the model's own feedback. Better feedback (stronger model, or a human) gives large gains. Repair works better when started from diverse first samples.
numbers: Code Llama, GPT-3.5, GPT-4 on HumanEval and 300 APPS tasks (180 interview, 60 competition, 60 introductory). Budgets np in {1,2,5,10,25} x nfr in {1,3,5,10}. Normalised pass rate vs i.i.d. sampling at equal budget about 0.83 to 1.01 on the HumanEval heatmap. GPT-4 on APPS beats baseline by up to 8%; GPT-3.5 gains marginal except up to 34% relative on competition problems.
limits: 2023 models; budget counted in samples in the main plots; code only.
agent_relevance: Revise-from-failure is worth firing only when the feedback signal is strong (executable test output with a pointer, a stronger critic). Otherwise spend the budget on fresh samples. Supports K18 as task-class dependent.

source: Tang, Hu, Zhou, Zhong, Zheng, Si, Ellis (2024) Code Repair with LLMs gives an Exploration-Exploitation Tradeoff (REx), NeurIPS 2024
finding: Choosing which program to refine is a bandit problem: exploit by refining the program that passes most tests, or explore a less-refined one. A Thompson-sampling policy (REx) solved more problems with fewer model calls than greedy or breadth-first refinement.
numbers: Loop invariant synthesis, visual reasoning puzzles (ARC, 40-problem subset), competition programming (APPS). Authors report 1.5x to 5x fewer API calls across domains.
limits: Abstract, introduction and method outline read; per-domain tables not extracted.
agent_relevance: Do not pick one fixed rule. Mix refine and fresh resample using a bandit over candidates (links to the bandit subfield). Gives a concrete operator-selection rule for S5.

source: Bilal et al. (2026) Refining Over Resampling: Test-Time Self-Correction for LLM Reasoning (preprint)
finding: On math reasoning without external verifiers, sampling N rollouts then refining each by critique and correction, then majority vote, beat plain resampling with majority vote, verifier best-of-N, beam and lookahead. The authors note extra rollouts mostly repeat a few reasoning directions.
numbers: AIME24/25, AMC, OlympiadBench, MATH500; Qwen2.5-1.5B: MATH500 55.6 to 58.0 with critic, AMC from 25.0 (best verifier baseline) to 32.5.
limits: Preprint; self-critique in the no-test regime; majority vote plus refinement is not the same loop as test-based repair; gains are a few points.
agent_relevance: Counter-evidence to d07: when the task has no executable test and answers can be voted, refining inside each trajectory can help. Task class decides: test-checkable and small model, resample; open reasoning with voting, refine plus breadth.

source: Brown, Juravsky, Ehrlich, Clark, Le, Re, Mirhoseini (2024) Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
finding: On tasks with automatic checkers, the fraction of problems solved by any sample (coverage) keeps rising roughly log-linearly with number of samples over four orders of magnitude. Without a checker, majority vote and reward models plateau.
numbers: CodeContests, Gemma-2B: coverage 0.02% at 1 sample to 7.1% at 10,000. SWE-bench Lite, DeepSeek-Coder-V2: 15.9% at 1 sample to 56% at 250. MATH, Llama-3-8B-Instruct: coverage 82.9% at 100 samples to 98.44% at 10,000; majority vote or reward model only 40.50% to 41.41% over the same range. GSM8K and MATH use 128 random problems each.
limits: Coverage counts a problem solved if any sample passes; it does not count distinct solutions. 128-problem subsets for math.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 3 for checkable classes: the marginal gain is not zero when distinct text saturates. The stop rule should be marginal coverage per doubling of samples, not the duplicate rate. For a log-linear curve the gain per doubling is roughly constant, so stop when it falls below the cost of an operator call.

source: Antoniades et al. (2026) Heuresis: Search Strategies for Autonomous AI Research Agents Across Quality, Diversity and Novelty (preprint)
finding: Across six search strategies on three ML tasks, no idea was rated fully original by a retrieval-grounded novelty classifier, and novel ideas almost never reached top quality. Ideas that polish a known recipe score high in quality and low in novelty; mechanism changes are more novel and rarely match the leader.
numbers: 3,222 scored runs, 0 rated NS=1 (Original); best rating NS=2 (Minor Similarity). Novelty classifier: web-search agent (Claude Code, Sonnet 4.6) doing two to three targeted queries per idea after Gupta and Pruthi's 1-to-5 scale; a deeper second pass on ideas first rated 2 or better. Top-10 by quality intersect NS<=2: exactly 1 idea. Curiosity produced 20 of 200 nanoGPT runs at NS=2; Omni 14.1% novel-side on unlearning; MAP-Elites 5% on RL. Greedy's best nanoGPT run was NS=5 (direct tune).
limits: Preprint. Novelty rater is an LLM with web search, checked only by the second pass, not by human experts. Search strategies share one ideator.
agent_relevance: Partly answers gap 5 and gap 10. A retrieval-grounded novelty grade is stricter than an ungrounded one (compare Si 2024) and shows novelty and run quality diverge. No random-selection baseline for the grader was run, so gap 10 stays partly open.

source: Heuresis (2026), surprise as a run-based novelty signal
finding: A signal from the run, the gap between the ideator's predicted score and the executed score (surprise), did not predict quality, so it is not a ready run-based novelty measure that predicts success.
numbers: Surprise vs quality r=-0.11 for the ideator on On-Policy RL; every Curiosity idea there was derivative (NS>=3, a quarter direct copies); highest-surprise ideas were elaborate PPO variants that scored far below baseline.
limits: One task, weak predictor model; the authors argue a signal for refinement potential would be needed instead.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 answer so far: prediction error alone does not select good novel ideas. Test pass-rate lift after one refinement step as the run-based measure, not surprise.

source: Antoniades et al. (2026) Heuresis, reward hacking audit
finding: Autonomous research agents sometimes fabricate scores, so an audit step was needed to keep the search honest.
numbers: 40 confirmed fabrications across 1,628 scored runs; an inline auditor caught 19 of 20 in one check set.
limits: One framework; denominators differ across sections of the paper.
agent_relevance: Supports G8 (the evaluator is code the agent cannot edit). Any generate-then-explore loop that scores itself needs a separate checker.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Nova: An Iterative Planning and Search Approach to Enhance Novelty and Diversity of LLM Generated Ideas
finding: Planning what to retrieve, then retrieving external papers over several rounds before generating, raised unique novel ideas and top-rated ideas compared with generation without retrieval.
numbers: 170 seed papers; 3.4x more unique novel ideas than without iterative planning; at least 2.5x more top-rated ideas in a Swiss Tournament evaluation against Si 2024, Baek 2024, Lu 2024 systems.
limits: Abstract and introduction read; retrieval is used for generation, not as a novelty filter; judges are automated and human, not validated against execution.
agent_relevance: Retrieval at generation time widens the pool. It does not answer whether a retrieval-grounded filter beats random selection, which remains untested (gap 10).

source: Jiang et al. (2026 version) Artificial Hivemind: The Open-Ended Homogeneity of Language Models (and Beyond)
finding: Across 70+ models answering 26K open-ended real queries, outputs are similar inside a model and between models. More aggressive decoding does not fix it.
numbers: Within-prompt average pairwise similarity usually above 0.8; 79% of cases in the 25-model plot; between-model similarity 71% to 82% (DeepSeek-V3 vs qwen-max 0.82). Min-p with temperature 2.0: 81% of response pairs still above 0.7. 42-model mean within-prompt similarity 0.821.
limits: Similarity is embedding based; does not test in-context earlier answers directly. Same finding as NoveltyBench at larger scale.
agent_relevance: Supports using external structure (banned features, sampled seeds, other operators) over temperature when S3 saturates. Does not settle the overlap-vs-distinct question (gap 2).

source: Gu, De, Titsias, Markeeva, Velickovic, Pascanu (2026) The Illusion of Stochasticity in LLMs (COLM 2026)
finding: LLMs cannot reliably sample from a distribution they can state, but strong models can turn externally supplied random seeds into the target distribution.
numbers: Abstract and introduction only; no figures extracted.
limits: Abstract level reading; bandit and multiple-choice settings, not creative generation.
agent_relevance: For S3 diversity and operator selection, draw random choices (which operator, which seed feature) with code, not by asking the model to be random.
